title: Magnets: why a pin jumps to a magnet

summary.text: A magnet pulls iron without touching it. It also pulls most steel, nickel and cobalt. It does not pull wood, plastic, paper or most other metals. The pull comes from inside the iron. Each tiny bit of iron is a tiny magnet. In a magnet, these tiny magnets all point the same way, so their pulls add up. In an ordinary nail, they point in different directions, so their pulls cancel out. Long ago, people in China, India, Greece and the Islamic world used magnet stones to steer ships. The whole Earth is a giant magnet too. Turtles, birds and even some bacteria can feel it. Nobody knows yet exactly how some animals feel it.
summary.art: A zoom picture: a child holding a magnet over a safety pin; inside the pin, rows of tiny arrows; beyond, the whole Earth with curved lines looping from pole to pole and a sea turtle swimming along them.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold a magnet near a steel safety pin. Move it closer very slowly, and stop just before they touch. Did the pin jump? Nothing touched it. So what reached across that gap?
intro.text: People have asked that question for thousands of years. In Sanskrit, a magnet is called chumbaka, which means 'the kisser'. An old Chinese book from about 2,250 years ago calls it the 'loving stone' that calls iron to come. Both names tell the same story. A magnet seems to want iron. In this unit we find out what is really happening. We go deep inside the iron, down to its atoms. Then we go out to the whole Earth, which is a magnet too.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a dark magnet stone a finger-width above a safety pin that is just lifting off a table, with a dotted line showing the gap.

outcomes: I can say which materials a magnet pulls: iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt. I can also say that most other metals, like copper, brass and aluminium, are not pulled.
I can make a magnet by stroking a needle, and use it as a compass. I can say why it points north.
I can run a fair test to compare how strong magnets are, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain that every electron is a tiny magnet, and that iron is magnetic because its tiny magnets line up in teams called domains.
I can tell the story of the magnet stone, lodestone, in India, China, Greece and the Islamic world.
I can explain that the Earth is a giant magnet made by moving liquid iron deep inside it, and that its magnet wanders and sometimes flips.
I can give examples of living things that sense the Earth's magnet, and say what scientists still do not know about it.

terms.meaning: A thing that pulls iron towards it, without touching it. A magnet can also push or pull another magnet.
terms.example: A fridge magnet holds a list on the fridge door, because the door has iron in it.
terms.art: A horseshoe magnet with three paper clips hanging from its ends.

terms.meaning: To pull something towards you. Magnets attract iron.
terms.example: A magnet attracts a steel pin across a small gap.
terms.art: A pin sliding across a table towards a magnet, with an arrow showing the pull.

terms.meaning: A material that a magnet pulls. The main ones are iron, most kinds of steel, nickel and cobalt.
terms.example: An iron nail and a steel safety pin are magnetic materials.
terms.art: A nail, a safety pin and a steel key all stuck to one magnet.

terms.meaning: A material that a magnet does not pull, as far as we can feel.
terms.example: Wood, plastic, glass, paper, copper, brass and aluminium are non-magnetic.
terms.art: A magnet lying next to a wooden pencil, a copper coin, a plastic spoon and a brass key, none of them moving.

terms.meaning: Iron mixed with a little of other things, to make it stronger. Most steel is magnetic. Some stainless steel, used for kitchen vessels, is not.
terms.example: A steel almirah holds a magnet. Some steel tumblers do not.
terms.art: A steel almirah with a magnet stuck on it and a steel tumbler with a magnet sliding off.

terms.meaning: One of the two ends of a magnet, where the pull is strongest. One end is called the north pole and the other the south pole.
terms.example: Dip a bar magnet in paper clips. Most clips cling to the two ends.
terms.art: A bar magnet with clusters of paper clips at both ends and almost none in the middle.

terms.meaning: A small magnet that can turn freely. It turns until one end points north.
terms.example: Sailors and hikers use a compass to find their way when they cannot see the Sun or the stars.
terms.art: A round compass with its needle pointing to N.

terms.meaning: To turn a piece of iron or steel into a magnet. One way is to stroke it with a magnet, many times, always in the same direction.
terms.example: Stroke a sewing needle 50 times with a magnet. Now the needle can pick up a pin.
terms.art: A hand stroking a magnet along a sewing needle in one direction, with curved arrows showing the stroke and lift.

terms.meaning: A natural magnet. It is a dark rock made of a mineral called magnetite, which has iron in it. Some pieces of it are magnets, straight out of the ground.
terms.example: Long ago, people in China, India and Greece found lodestones that picked up iron.
terms.art: A lumpy dark grey stone with iron nails bristling from it.

terms.meaning: A black mineral made of iron and oxygen. A magnet pulls it. Tiny grains of it are in most sand and soil.
terms.example: Drag a magnet through dry sand. The black grains that cling to it are magnetite.
terms.art: A magnet wrapped in a plastic bag, covered with a beard of tiny black grains.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: An iron nail, your hand and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a nail to a speck of iron to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: An even tinier bit on the outside of every atom. Every electron is also a tiny magnet, with its own north and south.
terms.example: Every atom in your body has electrons. In you, their tiny magnets point every which way and cancel out.
terms.art: An atom with little dots around it, each dot carrying a tiny arrow.

terms.meaning: The name scientists give to the tiny magnet built into every electron. Electrons are not really spinning like tops. Spin is just something every electron has, like it has electric charge.
terms.example: Two electrons that share a home in an atom usually point their spins opposite ways, so their tiny magnets cancel.
terms.art: Two dots side by side in an atom, one with an arrow up and one with an arrow down.

terms.meaning: A tiny patch inside iron where millions of atoms all point their tiny magnets the same way. Each domain is a team.
terms.example: In a plain nail, the teams point in different directions and cancel out. In a magnet, most teams point the same way.
terms.art: A square of iron divided into patches, each patch full of arrows pointing one way, the patches pointing different ways.

terms.meaning: The space around a magnet where its pull can be felt. We cannot see it, but iron grains and compasses show its shape.
terms.example: Sprinkle black sand on paper over a magnet and tap it. The grains line up in curved lines.
terms.art: Curved lines looping from one end of a bar magnet to the other, drawn in iron grains on paper.

terms.meaning: A piece of iron that acts as a magnet only while a magnet is near it.
terms.example: A paper clip hanging from a magnet can hold another clip. Take the magnet away and the clips drop.
terms.art: A chain of four paper clips hanging from a magnet, the bottom one just holding on.

terms.meaning: A magnet that keeps its pull for a long time, by itself.
terms.example: A fridge magnet, a bar magnet and a lodestone are permanent magnets.
terms.art: A bar magnet, a fridge magnet and a lodestone side by side.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a magnet stops being a magnet, because the heat shakes its tiny magnets out of line. For iron it is about 770 degrees Celsius, when iron glows red.
terms.example: A magnetised needle held in a gas flame until it glows red is no longer a magnet once it cools.
terms.art: Tongs holding a red-hot needle over a blue gas flame, with tiny arrows inside it scattering.

terms.meaning: The centre of the Earth, about 3,000 kilometres under our feet. It is mostly iron and nickel. The outer part is liquid metal and the inner part is solid.
terms.example: Moving liquid iron in the outer core makes the Earth into a giant magnet.
terms.art: The Earth cut open like a mango: a thin crust, a thick rocky middle, a glowing orange liquid layer and a bright solid ball at the centre.

terms.meaning: Coloured lights in the night sky, mostly near the North and South Poles. They glow when bits from the Sun crash into the air, guided by the Earth's magnet.
terms.example: In May 2024, red auroras were photographed from Hanle in Ladakh.
terms.art: Green and red curtains of light over snowy mountains under a starry sky.

terms.meaning: The ability of some living things to feel the Earth's magnet and use it to find their way. Scientists call it magnetoreception.
terms.example: Young sea turtles use it to find their way across the ocean.
terms.art: A baby sea turtle swimming in the dark ocean, with faint curved field lines around it.

explanations.definition: A magnet pulls iron, most kinds of steel, nickel and cobalt. These are called magnetic materials. A magnet does not pull wood, plastic, glass, paper or cloth, or most other metals.
explanations.description: Many people think a magnet pulls every metal. It does not. Copper, brass, aluminium, gold and silver are all metals, and a magnet ignores them. Steel is mostly iron, so most steel is pulled. Some stainless steel, used for kitchen vessels, is made in a special way and is hardly pulled at all. A magnet's pull also goes through things. It can pull a pin through paper, cloth, wood or water. And the pull gets weaker very fast as you move further away.
examples: A magnet sticks to a steel almirah but not to a brass diya.
A magnet can drag a paper clip along the underside of a table, through the wood.
A one-rupee coin may or may not stick, depending on what metal it is made of. Test yours.
explanations.art: A magnet surrounded by everyday things: a nail, a pin and a steel key stuck to it; a brass diya, a copper vessel, an aluminium foil ball and a plastic spoon left behind.
explanations.context: This card says which things a magnet pulls, and which it does not. Many people are surprised that most metals are not pulled.

explanations.concept: Every electron is a tiny magnet
explanations.definition: Every atom has tiny bits on its outside called electrons. Every electron is itself a tiny magnet, with a north and a south. Scientists call this tiny magnet the electron's spin.
explanations.description: So why isn't everything a magnet? Because electrons in an atom usually live in pairs. In each pair, one electron points its tiny magnet one way, and the other points the opposite way. The two cancel out, like two children pulling a rope equally hard in opposite directions. Nothing moves. That is what happens in wood, plastic, water, copper and you. In a few kinds of atoms, like iron, some electrons have no partner. Their tiny magnets are not cancelled. So each iron atom is a little magnet.
examples: In a copper atom, all the electrons but one are in pairs, and that last one is shared with the other copper atoms. So copper is not magnetic.
An iron atom has four electrons without partners. So every iron atom is a tiny magnet.
explanations.art: Two atoms side by side: on the left, pairs of up and down arrows cancelling; on the right, an iron atom with four lonely arrows all pointing up.
explanations.context: This card zooms right inside atoms, to find where a magnet's pull really comes from.

explanations.definition: Inside iron, the tiny atom-magnets line up with their neighbours in patches called domains. Each domain is a team of millions of atoms all pointing the same way.
explanations.description: In a plain iron nail, there are many domains. They point in different directions, so their pulls cancel out. The nail is not a magnet. Bring a magnet near, and the domains turn to line up with it. Now the nail is a magnet too, for as long as the magnet is near. That is why one paper clip hanging from a magnet can hold another clip. In a permanent magnet, most domains stay lined up by themselves. The French scientist Pierre Weiss guessed that domains exist in 1907. In 1931 the American scientist Francis Bitter first showed their edges, using very fine iron powder in oil under a microscope. Why do iron's tiny magnets want to point like their neighbours? The answer comes from quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things.
examples: A chain of paper clips hangs from a magnet. Each clip becomes a temporary magnet that holds the next one.
Stroke a needle with a magnet and its domains line up. Now the needle is a magnet.
explanations.art: Two squares of iron: on the left, patches of arrows pointing every which way, labelled 'nail'; on the right, nearly all the patches pointing the same way, labelled 'magnet'.
explanations.context: Why is a nail not a magnet, even though every iron atom is a tiny magnet? This card explains the teams of tiny magnets inside iron.

explanations.concept: Making a magnet, and breaking one
explanations.definition: You can make a magnet by lining up the domains in iron or steel. You can break a magnet by shaking them out of line again, with heat or hard knocks.
explanations.description: Stroke a steel needle with a magnet, 50 times, always the same way. Each stroke tugs more domains into line, and the needle becomes a magnet. Nothing was added to the needle. Nothing was taken away. Only the line-up changed. Heat does the opposite. Heat is really atoms jiggling. Heat iron until it glows red, at about 770 degrees Celsius, and the atoms jiggle so hard that they cannot stay lined up. The magnet is gone. This temperature is called the Curie point, after Pierre Curie, who studied it in 1895. Marie Curie's very first research, in 1897, was on magnets too. She measured how well many kinds of steel could hold their magnetism, before she went on to discover radium.
examples: Dropping or hammering a magnet many times can weaken it, because the knocks shake the domains.
Old soft-iron nails lose their magnetism quickly. Hard steel, like a needle, keeps it for days or weeks.
explanations.art: Three panels: a needle being stroked by a magnet with its arrows lining up; the needle picking up a pin; the needle red-hot in a flame with its arrows scattered.
explanations.context: Can you turn a needle into a magnet? Can you turn a magnet back into plain iron? This card explains how, and why.

explanations.concept: What is an electron's spin, really?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that every electron has a tiny magnet built in, called spin. They can measure it very exactly. But what is it, underneath? People have given different answers, and the question is still argued about.
examples: In 1922, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach sent silver atoms flying between magnets. The atoms split into just two streams, not a smear. Something inside each atom could only point 'up' or 'down'.
Nobody has ever seen an electron, or watched it turn.

perspectives.who: George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit, two young scientists in the Netherlands, in 1925
perspectives.explanation: The electron is a tiny ball of charge spinning like a top. A spinning charge makes a magnet. That is how spin got its name.
The electron cannot really be a spinning ball. Its surface would have to move faster than light. Spin is just a basic property of every electron, like its charge. It does not need anything under it.

perspectives.who: The physicist Richard Feynman, in a 1983 BBC interview
perspectives.explanation: When we ask 'why do magnets pull?', each answer leads to another 'why'. At some point we can only say: this is how the world behaves. Some physicists and philosophers think that is not a real answer, and keep looking.

explanations.art: A tiny glowing dot with a question mark, and two thought bubbles: one showing a spinning top, one showing just an arrow.
explanations.context: Every electron is a tiny magnet. This card asks a question scientists still argue about: what is that tiny magnet, underneath?

explanations.concept: Magnetism and electricity are one force
explanations.definition: Magnetism and electricity are two sides of one force, which scientists call the electromagnetic force. Moving electric charge makes a magnet, and a moving magnet makes electricity.
explanations.description: In 1820, a Danish scientist, Hans Christian Oersted, noticed that a compass needle twitched when electricity flowed in a wire nearby. The electric current was making a magnet. Michael Faraday, who had left school at 13, then found the reverse in 1831. Moving a magnet in a coil of wire makes electricity. In 1865, James Clerk Maxwell wrote down the rules of both in one set of equations. He found that light itself is a wave of electricity and magnetism. Later, in 1905, Albert Einstein showed that magnetism is what electric pushes and pulls look like when charges move. The same force also holds atoms together and makes friction.
examples: A doorbell, a fan and a mixer all have electric magnets inside.
Every power station spins magnets near coils of wire to make electricity.
Light from the Sun is a wave of electricity and magnetism.
explanations.art: A compass needle twitching next to a wire connected to a battery, and beside it a sunbeam drawn as a wavy line labelled 'electric and magnetic'.
explanations.context: This card links magnets to electricity and to light. They turn out to be one force.

explanations.concept: Lodestone: the stone that finds iron
explanations.definition: A lodestone is a natural magnet. It is a piece of a black mineral called magnetite, which is made of iron and oxygen. Many cultures found lodestones long ago.
explanations.description: In Greece, about 2,600 years ago, the thinker Thales is said to have wondered whether a lodestone has a soul, because it moves iron. In China, a book from about 240 BCE, the Lüshi Chunqiu, says the loving stone calls iron to come. In India, the magnet was called ayaskanta, which means 'beloved of iron', and chumbaka, 'the kisser'. The Sushruta Samhita, an old Indian book of surgery, describes using a magnet to pull a smooth iron arrowhead out of a wound. Later, people learned to steer by magnets. A Chinese military book from 1044, the Wujing Zongyao, describes an iron 'south-pointing fish' floated in water. In 1088, the Chinese scholar Shen Kuo described a magnetised needle. He also noticed that it does not point exactly north. Around 1232, Muhammad al-Awfi, a writer at the court of Delhi, described sailors floating an iron fish rubbed with a magnet to find their way. In Europe, Petrus Peregrinus described a magnet's two poles in 1269.
examples: Lodestones were set in brass or silver caps, so people could carry them and rub needles with them.
Iron fish compasses floated in a bowl of water, like the needle compass in this unit's experiment.
explanations.art: A world map with little pictures: a lodestone in Greece, a floating iron fish in China, a surgeon with a magnet in India, a ship with a bowl of water in the Arabian Sea.
explanations.context: Who first found magnets, and what did they do with them? This card tells the story of the lodestone across the world.

explanations.description: Most magnetite is not a magnet. Only a few pieces are lodestones. The Earth's own magnet is far too weak to make such a strong magnet. So where did lodestones get their pull? Scientists have different ideas.
examples: Lodestones are usually found near the surface of the ground, not deep inside it.
A lightning strike carries a huge electric current, and electric currents make magnets.

perspectives.who: Peter Wasilewski and Gunther Kletetschka, scientists in the USA, in 1999
perspectives.explanation: Lightning did it. When lightning strikes the ground, its huge current makes a strong magnet for a moment. That can line up the domains in magnetite nearby.
Lightning explains some lodestones, but maybe not all. The kind of magnetite matters too. Some magnetite holds a line-up much better than others. The full answer is still being studied.

explanations.art: A lightning bolt striking a rocky hillside, with a glowing patch of black stone where it hit.
explanations.context: Lodestones are natural magnets. This card asks how they got their pull, which scientists are still working out.

explanations.concept: The Earth is a giant magnet
explanations.definition: The whole Earth is a magnet. Its magnet is made by liquid iron moving in the Earth's outer core, about 3,000 kilometres under our feet.
explanations.description: In 1600, an English doctor, William Gilbert, made a ball out of lodestone. He called it a 'little Earth'. He moved a tiny compass over it, and the compass behaved just as compasses do on the real Earth. So he said the Earth itself is a magnet. That is why a compass points north. Today we know more. The Earth's centre is mostly iron and nickel. The outer part of the core is liquid metal, hotter than the surface of the Sun. It swirls slowly as the Earth spins. Moving metal carries electric currents, and electric currents make magnets. In 1936, a Danish scientist, Inge Lehmann, studied earthquake waves passing through the Earth. She found that the very centre is solid, a ball inside the liquid. A compass does not point exactly at the North Pole. It points at the magnetic north pole, which is some distance away.
examples: Hang a magnetised needle on a thread, far from any iron. It turns until it points north and south.
In most of India, a compass points only a degree or two away from true north. In Canada, it can point far off.
explanations.art: The Earth cut open, its glowing liquid outer core swirling, with curved magnetic lines looping out of the south and back in at the north, and a tiny compass on the surface.
explanations.context: Why does a compass point north? This card explains that the whole Earth is a magnet, and what makes it one.

explanations.concept: The Earth's magnet wanders and flips
explanations.definition: The Earth's magnet is not fixed. Its magnetic north pole moves every year. Every so often, over hundreds of thousands of years, the whole magnet flips, so that a compass would point south.
explanations.description: When hot lava cools into rock, tiny magnetite grains in it line up with the Earth's magnet, then freeze in place. So old rocks are a record of where the Earth's magnet pointed. In 1906, a French scientist, Bernard Brunhes, found rocks magnetised the 'wrong' way. In 1929, a Japanese scientist, Motonori Matuyama, showed from rocks in Japan and Korea that the Earth's magnet has flipped many times. The last flip was about 780,000 years ago. Today the magnetic north pole is moving from Canada towards Siberia, tens of kilometres every year. India has watched the Earth's magnet for a long time. An observatory at Colaba in Bombay began measuring it in 1841. In 1904 it moved to Alibag, because Bombay's new electric trams would have disturbed the measurements. Its records are still kept.
examples: The Colaba observatory recorded a huge magnetic storm in 1859, when auroras were seen over much of the world.
Stripes of rock on the ocean floor are magnetised one way, then the other, like a barcode of flips.
explanations.art: A long ribbon of ocean-floor rock in stripes, each stripe with a little compass needle, the needles taking turns pointing north and south.
explanations.context: The Earth's magnet sounds like it should stay still. This card shows that it wanders, and sometimes flips right over.

chart.title: How we learned that the Earth's magnet changes
rows: A compass needle does not point exactly north.
Began measuring the Earth's magnet every day.
Some rocks are magnetised the 'wrong' way.
The Earth's magnet has flipped many times.
The Earth's very centre is solid metal.

explanations.concept: The Earth's magnet shields us, and makes auroras
explanations.definition: The Earth's magnet reaches far out into space. It turns aside most of the fast, tiny bits that stream out from the Sun, called the solar wind.
explanations.description: The Sun blows out a steady wind of tiny charged bits. Charged bits are steered by magnets. So the Earth's magnet bends most of the solar wind around our planet. Some bits are led down towards the North and South Poles. There they crash into the air high above us and make it glow. These glowing curtains of light are auroras. When the Sun has a big storm, auroras can be seen much further from the poles. In May 2024, cameras at the Indian Astronomical Observatory in Hanle, Ladakh, photographed a red aurora. Mars has almost no magnet around the whole planet today. Many scientists think that, without one, the solar wind slowly stripped away much of Mars's air.
examples: Big solar storms can disturb compasses, radio and satellites.
Auroras are green, red and sometimes purple, depending on which gas in the air glows.
explanations.art: The Earth with its magnetic field drawn as a bubble, the solar wind streaming from the Sun and bending around it, and small green auroras at the poles.
explanations.context: What does the Earth's magnet do for the planet? This card explains the shield it makes, and the lights in the sky.

explanations.concept: Living things that feel the Earth's magnet
explanations.description: Many animals seem to use the Earth's magnet to find their way. For some, scientists have strong proof. How they feel it is still argued about.
examples: Some bacteria, living things far too small to see, grow a chain of tiny magnetite crystals inside them. The chain works like a compass needle, so they swim along the Earth's magnetic lines. Salvatore Bellini saw them in Italy in 1963, but his notes were not published. Richard Blakemore described them in the USA in 1975.

Kenneth and Catherine Lohmann have shown that young loggerhead sea turtles can tell where they are in the ocean from the strength and slant of the Earth's magnet. Olive ridley turtles nest on Odisha's beaches, and may do the same, but nobody has tested them as carefully.
In 1972, Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko showed that European robins, small birds, still pick the right way to migrate inside a closed room, using only the Earth's magnet.

perspectives.explanation: Birds see the magnet with their eyes. Light hits a special substance in the eye, called cryptochrome, and makes pairs of electrons whose spins are affected by the Earth's magnet. In 2021, a team led by Jingjing Xu and Henrik Mouritsen showed that robin cryptochrome responds to magnets in the lab.

Some animals may carry tiny magnetite crystals, like the bacteria do. For a while, iron-rich cells in pigeon beaks looked like the answer. In 2012, careful tests showed those cells were blood cleaner cells, not magnet sensors. The search goes on.

In 2019, Connie Wang, Joseph Kirschvink and others reported that some people's brainwaves changed when a magnet was turned around them. They did not feel anything. Other scientists say this needs to be tested again before we believe it.

explanations.art: A night scene: a robin in a cage looking up, a turtle hatchling heading into the sea, and a magnified bacterium with a chain of tiny black crystals inside.
explanations.context: Can living things feel the Earth's magnet? This card is about those that can, and the open question of how.

explanations.concept: Everything answers a magnet, a little
explanations.definition: Even 'non-magnetic' things react to a very strong magnet. Some are pulled a tiny bit, and some are pushed away a tiny bit.
explanations.description: Water, wood, plastic and you are pushed away from a magnet. The push is far too weak to feel with a home magnet. In a giant lab magnet, it is strong enough to make a live frog float in the air. Andre Geim and Michael Berry did this in the Netherlands in 1997. The frog was unharmed. Some things are pulled a little, too. Liquid oxygen, very cold, clings between the ends of a strong magnet. So 'magnetic' and 'non-magnetic' are not two separate kinds of stuff. They are big and tiny amounts of the same thing.
examples: A strong magnet held near a floating grape on a needle can make it turn a little away. This needs a very strong magnet.
Liquid oxygen hangs between the ends of a strong magnet like a little bridge.
explanations.art: A small green frog floating calmly in the air inside a tall magnet tube, with lines of the magnetic field around it.
explanations.context: We call some things 'non-magnetic'. This card shows that, with a strong enough magnet, everything answers a little.

agreed.text: Magnets pull iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt. They do not pull most other materials, including most metals.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with a magnet at home. Scientists have tested thousands of materials in the lab.

agreed.text: A magnet's pull comes from electrons, which are each a tiny magnet. In iron, they line up in teams called domains.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can measure the tiny magnet of a single electron. They can also see domains under special microscopes and watch their edges move as a magnet comes near.

agreed.text: Iron and steel can be made into magnets, and magnets can be weakened by heat and knocks.
agreed.evidence: Stroke a needle and it picks up a pin. Heat it red-hot and it stops. Pierre Curie measured the exact temperatures in 1895.

agreed.text: The Earth is a magnet, made by moving liquid iron deep inside it. Its magnet has flipped many times.
agreed.evidence: Compasses point north everywhere on Earth. Earthquake waves show a liquid metal core. Old lava rocks are magnetised in both directions.

agreed.text: Some living things use the Earth's magnet to find their way.
agreed.evidence: Magnetic bacteria swim along magnetic lines. Young sea turtles and robins change direction when scientists change the magnet around them.

challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Most things a magnet sticks to around the house are metal, like the fridge, the almirah and pins.
challenging.against: Test a brass key, a copper vessel, aluminium foil or a gold ring. A magnet ignores them all. Only metals with iron, nickel or cobalt are pulled.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common mistake: that every metal is magnetic.

challenging.claim: A compass points to the North Pole, or to the Pole Star.
challenging.who: Many people, and many old books
challenging.for: A compass points roughly north, and the Pole Star is roughly north too.
challenging.against: A compass points to the magnetic north pole, which is not the same place as the North Pole, and which moves every year. Shen Kuo noticed the difference in China in 1088. The Pole Star has nothing to do with it.
challenging.context: Where exactly does a compass point? This card looks at a common answer that is not quite right.

challenging.claim: Magnets were discovered by a shepherd called Magnes, whose iron-nailed sandals stuck to a rock.
challenging.who: A legend told by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, about 1,950 years ago
challenging.for: It is a good story, and the word 'magnet' does sound like 'Magnes'.
challenging.against: There is no evidence the shepherd was real. Most experts think the word comes from Magnesia, a region in Greece and Turkey where lodestones were found. And people in China and India knew lodestones too.
challenging.context: Where does the word 'magnet' come from? This card looks at an old legend.

challenging.claim: Indian sailors invented the compass, using an iron fish floating in oil called a matsya yantra.
challenging.who: Some writers in the 1900s, and many websites
challenging.for: Indian Ocean sailors did use floating iron fish compasses. Al-Awfi, writing at the Delhi court around 1232, describes one.
challenging.against: No old Indian text has been found that describes a matsya yantra compass. The oldest clear written descriptions of magnetic compasses are Chinese, from 1044 and 1088. Ideas probably travelled along the trade routes.
challenging.context: Who invented the compass? This card looks at a claim often made about India, and what the evidence says.

challenging.claim: Cows and deer line up north and south as they graze, because they feel the Earth's magnet.
challenging.who: Sabine Begall and other scientists, studying satellite pictures, in 2008
challenging.for: In thousands of satellite pictures, grazing cattle seemed to face north or south more often than other ways.
challenging.against: In 2011, another team looked at new pictures and found no such pattern. Wind, sunlight and slopes also change which way cows face.
challenging.context: Do cows have a compass? This card is about a surprising claim that scientists still argue about.

challenging.claim: Magnet bracelets and magnet mats cure pain and illness.
challenging.who: Many sellers, in India and around the world
challenging.for: Some people say they feel better when they wear them.
challenging.against: Careful tests compare real magnets with fake ones that look the same. People feel about as much better with the fake ones. In 2007, a review of many such tests found no good evidence that magnets help pain. Feeling better because we expect to is real, but it is not the magnet.
challenging.context: Magnet bracelets are sold in many markets. This card looks at what tests show about them.

challenging.claim: People can sense the Earth's magnet.
challenging.who: Connie Wang, Joseph Kirschvink and others, in 2019
challenging.for: In a quiet test room, some people's brainwaves changed when a magnet was turned around them in one particular way.
challenging.against: Nobody in the test felt anything. Only some people showed it, and the result has not yet been repeated by other teams.
challenging.context: Birds and turtles feel the Earth's magnet. This card asks whether people might too.

big_questions.q: Every electron in your body is a tiny magnet. So why don't you stick to the fridge?
big_questions.hint: What happens when two children pull a rope equally hard in opposite directions?

big_questions.q: A magnet pulls a pin through paper, through wood, even through your hand. What is in the gap that does the pulling?
big_questions.hint: Scientists call it a field. Is an invisible field a 'thing'? Is empty space really empty?

big_questions.q: When you stroke a needle and it becomes a magnet, nothing is added and nothing is taken away. So what changed?
big_questions.hint: Think about a crowd of people facing every way, and then all facing the same way.

big_questions.q: The Earth's magnet has flipped many times. What might happen to birds and turtles during a flip?
big_questions.hint: Flips take thousands of years. Animals have lived through many of them.

big_questions.q: A turtle can find the beach where it hatched, across a whole ocean, without a map. What does a turtle know that we don't?
big_questions.hint: Do we sometimes think people are the cleverest animals only because we test the things we are good at?

big_questions.q: Tiny magnets that each point their own way cancel out. When they all point together, they make a pull. When does pulling together make a family, a class or a town stronger? When could it be a bad thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of a crowd that all runs one way. Is that always wise?

big_questions.q: Old names for the magnet mean 'the kisser', 'beloved of iron' and 'the loving stone'. Why do you think so many people thought of magnets as loving?
big_questions.hint: Is there a pull in your life that you can't see, but can feel?

big_questions.q: Marie Curie's first research was on magnets in steel. Many books mention Pierre Curie's magnet work, but not hers. Why might that be?
big_questions.hint: Who usually gets written down in history books? Who gets left out?

big_questions.q: The Earth's magnet shields us from the Sun's wind, and we never feel it. What else protects us that we never notice?
big_questions.hint: Think of the air, the ozone, the people who keep water clean.

big_questions.q: Scientists can measure an electron's spin very exactly, but can't say what it 'is'. Is it enough to know how something behaves, or do we need to know what it is?
big_questions.hint: Can you describe your best friend without knowing what they are made of?

story.title: The Iron Fish
story.note: Floating iron fish compasses rubbed with a lodestone are real: Muhammad al-Awfi, writing at the Delhi court around 1232, describes sailors using one, and ships really sailed between Khambhat in Gujarat and Aden. Amina, her mother, the pilot and this voyage are made up.
text: The ship was called the Swift Gazelle, and it smelled of cloves, tar and the sea. It had left Khambhat, in Gujarat, nine days ago. It was carrying cotton cloth and indigo to Aden, far across the Arabian Sea. Amina was ten. She was the only child on board, because her mother was the ship's cook.

Amina's favourite person on the ship, after her mother, was the pilot, old Yusuf. He knew the stars the way Amina knew the path to her grandmother's well. At night he sat with his chin up and his eyes half closed, reading the sky. He told the helmsman where to steer.

But Yusuf had a second way of finding the way. It lived in a wooden box near the back of the ship. Inside the box was a small brass bowl. Inside a silk bag was a lumpy black stone. And inside a fold of cloth was a fish, no longer than Amina's finger, cut from a thin sheet of iron.

On the fourth night, Yusuf had let her watch. He poured water into the brass bowl. He took out the black stone and rubbed it along the iron fish, from tail to nose. He lifted it away, and rubbed again, from tail to nose. Never back and forth. Always the same way. He counted under his breath, all the way to fifty. Then he laid the fish gently on the water, where it floated like a leaf.

The fish shivered. It turned slowly, as if it were sniffing the air, and then it stopped. Its nose pointed to the south. Amina turned the bowl. The fish turned back. She turned the bowl the other way. The fish turned back again, to the south, every time.
'It is hungry for the south,' said Yusuf. 'The stone teaches it. You will not need it often. But when the clouds come, the fish is the only one on this ship who still knows the way.'

Amina also learned what else the black stone could do. In the galley, the ship's tiny kitchen, she held it near her mother's iron ladle. The ladle leapt to the stone with a click. The stone ignored the brass cups, the clay pots and the wooden spoons. It wanted only iron.
On the eleventh day, the clouds came.

They came low and grey, and then black. The wind rose and the rain hit the deck like thrown rice. That night there were no stars at all. The ship rolled so hard that her mother tied the big iron cooking pot, the deg, to the back wall with a rope, right beside Yusuf's wooden box, so it could not slide about and break someone's leg.
Yusuf brought out the brass bowl. He floated the iron fish. Its nose swung round and settled. He called his direction to the helmsman, and the ship turned.

For a long time, nobody spoke. Amina sat wrapped in a blanket, watching the fish by the light of a little oil lamp. Something was wrong, and it took her a while to see what it was. The fish was not pointing where it had pointed on the fourth night. It was pointing at the back wall of the ship. It was pointing at the deg.

Her heart thumped. She thought of the ladle leaping to the stone. If the stone wanted iron, did the fish want iron too? She took the lamp, crept to the back wall, and moved the lamp past the big pot. Then she held her mother's iron ladle near the bowl. The fish swung towards the ladle as if it had been called.
'Yusuf,' she whispered. Then louder, 'Yusuf! The fish is looking at the pot!'

The pilot frowned. He looked at the bowl, at the pot, at the ladle in her hand. Then he said a word Amina's mother would not have liked, and shouted for two sailors to untie the deg and carry it to the front of the ship.
When the pot was gone, the fish shivered. It turned, slowly, slowly, nearly a quarter of the way round. And there it stopped, pointing to the south.

Yusuf looked at it for a long time. 'We have been steering towards a cooking pot,' he said at last. 'For half the night.' He called the new direction to the helmsman. The Swift Gazelle leaned, creaked and turned.

But the fish seemed lazy now, slow to turn and quick to wander. Yusuf's hands were shaking with cold. So Amina opened the silk bag and took out the black stone. From tail to nose. Lift away. From tail to nose. Never back and forth. She counted to fifty, as she had heard him count. When she floated the fish again, it swung round at once, quick and sure.

In the grey morning, the rain stopped. The sailors leaned over the rail and pointed. Beside the ship, in the dark water, swam three sea turtles, heading the same way the ship was going. They had no bowl, no stone and no iron fish. They swam steadily on, as if they had never been lost at all.
'How do they know the way?' Amina asked.
Yusuf watched them go. 'I have sailed for forty years,' he said, 'and I have never once known.'

Two days later they saw the brown mountains behind Aden. After that, on every voyage, the big iron deg travelled at the front of the ship. And every night, in the fold of cloth beside the brass bowl, the black stone and the iron fish lay waiting for a girl who knew the way to rub them.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the fish is a magnet, and a magnet pulls iron. So the big iron cooking pot pulled the fish's nose towards it, and the ship steered towards the pot instead of south. Moving the iron away let the fish line up with the Earth's magnet again. Stroking it with the lodestone, always in one direction, lined up the tiny magnets inside the iron, so its pull grew strong again. The turtles at the end know the way without any iron at all, because their own bodies sense the Earth's magnet. Nobody yet fully knows how.
ask: Why did the iron fish point the wrong way during the storm?
How did Amina work out what was wrong? What had she seen in the galley?
Why did Yusuf rub the fish from tail to nose, and never back and forth?
The turtles found the way without a fish. How do you think they did it?
Amina was the cook's daughter, not a sailor, and she noticed what the pilot missed. Why do you think the person who notices is not always the person in charge?

games.title: Monsoon Voyage: sail by the iron fish
games.context: This is a board game about sailing across the Arabian Sea with a magnet compass. Players answer magnet questions to move their ship from Khambhat in Gujarat to Aden before the storm catches them.

printables.title: A sea board with 20 squares, from Khambhat to Aden
items: Square 0: Khambhat, the start
Squares 4, 9 and 15: CLOUDY NIGHT, no stars
Squares 6 and 13: IRON ANCHOR next to your compass
Square 11: TURTLES! Swim with them, move 2 squares
Square 20: Aden, the finish

printables.title: 24 question cards to cut out
items: Will a magnet pull a brass key? (No)
Will a magnet pull a steel safety pin? (Yes)
Name one metal a magnet pulls. (Iron, steel, nickel or cobalt)
Will a magnet pull aluminium foil? (No)
Can a magnet pull a pin through a page of paper? (Yes)
What do you rub a needle with to make it a magnet? (A magnet)
Rub the needle back and forth, or always one way? (Always one way)
Which way does a compass point? (North and south)
What is a natural magnet stone called? (A lodestone)
What is the black magnet mineral in sand called? (Magnetite)
What tiny bit inside every atom is a tiny magnet? (The electron)
What are the teams of tiny magnets inside iron called? (Domains)
Does heating a magnet red-hot make it stronger or take its magnet away? (Takes it away)
What makes the Earth a magnet? (Moving liquid iron deep inside it)
Has the Earth's magnet ever flipped? (Yes, many times)
Name an animal that feels the Earth's magnet. (Turtle, robin or magnetic bacteria)
What are the coloured lights near the poles called? (Auroras)
What does 'chumbaka' mean? (The kisser)
Who first said the Earth is a magnet, in 1600? (William Gilbert)
Who found that the Earth's centre is solid, in 1936? (Inge Lehmann)
TEST IT: does a magnet stick to your spoon? Guess first, then test.
TEST IT: how many paper clips can your magnet hold in a chain?
TEST IT: does a magnet pull a pin through your hand? Guess first.
TEST IT: put a coin on the table. Does a magnet pull it?

printables.title: One paper ship for each player, and one black storm cloud

rules: Put every ship on Khambhat, square 0. Put the storm cloud on Khambhat too.
On your turn, another player reads you the top question card. Playing alone? Read it yourself and check the answer in the brackets.
Answer right, and roll the dice and move that many squares. Answer wrong, and move just 1 square.
On a TEST IT card, do the test. Everyone who guessed right moves 2 squares.
CLOUDY NIGHT square: no stars to steer by. Say how a compass helps, then move on 1 square.
IRON ANCHOR square: your compass is fooled. Go back 2 squares, unless you can say what to do. The answer is: move the iron away from the compass.
After everyone has had a turn, the storm cloud moves 2 squares.
Reach Aden first to win. If the storm cloud lands on your ship or passes it, you must stop and shelter: miss one turn. Playing alone, try to reach Aden before the storm does.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the sea board. 2. Put each ship and the storm cloud on Khambhat. 3. Shuffle the question cards and put them face down.
flow.say: Long ago, ships sailed from Khambhat in Gujarat across the Arabian Sea to Aden. On cloudy nights there were no stars to steer by. Sailors used an iron fish rubbed with a magnet stone, floating in water. Let's sail.
flow.kid: Put your ship on Khambhat. Put the storm cloud there too. Mix up the cards. You are a sailor, steering by a magnet. Can you reach Aden before the storm?
flow.context: This is the first step of Monsoon Voyage. It is a board game where you sail a ship using magnet questions. Here you set up the board.

flow.do: Play the card 'Will a magnet pull a brass key?' as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Will a magnet pull a brass key?
flow.kid: Practice card. Will a magnet pull a brass key? Tap your answer.

check.q: Will a magnet pull a brass key?
options: Yes, because brass is a metal
No, brass has no iron in it
check.why: Brass is a metal made of copper and zinc. Neither is magnetic, so a magnet ignores brass. Picking 'yes' usually means thinking all metals are magnetic. Only metals with iron, nickel or cobalt in them are pulled.

flow.do: 1. Take turns: read a card, answer, then move. 2. Move the storm cloud 2 squares after each round. 3. Do the TEST IT cards together.
flow.say: Answer your card, then roll. Watch out for the iron anchor squares.
flow.kid: Answer your card. Right? Roll the dice and sail on. Wrong? Move one square. Then the storm moves 2.
flow.parent: The game is balanced so that a player who answers most cards right reaches Aden before the storm. If your child is getting many wrong, read the answer aloud after each card and let them try again next round. On the TEST IT card about a coin, the answer depends on the coin. Some Indian coins are made of ferritic stainless steel, which a magnet pulls. Others are not. That is a good surprise.

flow.do: When someone lands on an IRON ANCHOR square, stop and talk about it.
flow.say: Why does an iron anchor near the compass fool it?
flow.kid: Iron anchor! Your compass is fooled. Why? How do you fix it?

ask.q: Why does iron near a compass make it point the wrong way?
good: The compass is a magnet, and a magnet pulls iron.
The needle turns towards the iron instead of north.

check.q: Your compass points at an iron anchor instead of north. What do you do?
options: Shake the compass hard
Move the iron far away from the compass
Add more iron next to it
check.why: The compass needle is a magnet, and a magnet is pulled towards iron. Move the iron away and the needle can line up with the Earth's magnet again. Shaking the compass does not help, because the iron is still there pulling it.

flow.do: Finish the game and talk about the turtles square.
flow.say: On square 11, turtles helped you. Real sea turtles find their way across oceans, with no compass. How do you think they do it?
flow.kid: Who reached Aden? On square 11, turtles helped you. Real turtles cross oceans with no compass. How?
flow.think: Sailors needed an iron fish to find the way. Turtles need nothing but their own bodies. Who is the better navigator?

games.title: Magnet Says: be the tiny magnets
games.context: This is a listening game, like Simon Says. Every player is a tiny magnet inside iron. The caller shouts what happens to the iron, and the tiny magnets must do the right thing.

printables.title: 12 caller cards
items: MAGNET COMING! (everyone turns to face the caller)
MAGNET GONE, SOFT IRON! (everyone turns any way they like)
MAGNET GONE, HARD STEEL! (everyone stays facing the same way)
HEAT! RED-HOT! (everyone jiggles, then faces any way)
COPPER! (find a partner and stand back to back, frozen)
WOOD! (trick card: nothing happens, stand still)
PLASTIC! (trick card: nothing happens)
STROKE! (the caller walks past slowly, and each player turns to face the same way as the caller walks)
HAMMER! (everyone wobbles, and half turn around)
COMPASS! (everyone points to north)
BRASS! (trick card: nothing happens)
EARTH FLIP! (everyone points to south)

printables.title: For one child alone: a grid of 12 paper arrows to turn on a table
items: 12 arrows cut from card, each as long as a finger

rules: One person is the caller. Everyone else is a tiny magnet, an atom of iron. Stand around the room, facing any way.
The caller reads a card out loud. The tiny magnets must do what it says, fast.
Trick cards, like WOOD, mean do nothing at all. Anyone who moves is out for one round.
Anyone who does the wrong thing is out for one round. They can come back next round.
Playing alone: lay 12 paper arrows on the table, pointing every which way. Draw a card and turn the arrows to match it, as fast as you can. Count how many cards you get right out of 12.

flow.do: 1. Choose a caller. 2. Everyone else stands around the room facing any way. 3. Shuffle the caller cards.
flow.say: Inside iron, every atom is a tiny magnet. Right now you're facing every which way, like the atoms in a plain nail. Your pulls cancel out. The nail is not a magnet.
flow.kid: You are a tiny magnet inside iron. Face any way you like. Right now you all point different ways. So the iron is not a magnet. Listen to the caller.
flow.context: This is the first step of Magnet Says. It is a listening game where players act out the tiny magnets inside iron.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. Give the tiny magnets three seconds to act. Players who move on a trick card sit out one round.
flow.say: Magnet coming!
flow.kid: Listen to each card. Do what it says, fast. On WOOD, PLASTIC or BRASS, don't move at all!
flow.parent: After each card, say in one sentence what it means. 'Magnet coming' means a magnet lines up the domains. 'Soft iron' means a nail that loses its magnet as soon as the magnet goes. 'Hard steel' means a needle that keeps it. 'Copper' means electrons in pairs that cancel. Heat and hammering shake the line-up apart.

flow.do: After the game, count how many players faced the same way after STROKE, and after HEAT.
flow.say: After STROKE, you all faced the same way. After HEAT, you faced all over the place. Which one was a magnet?
flow.kid: After STROKE, did you all face the same way? After HEAT? Which time were you a magnet?

check.q: In the game, when were the tiny magnets acting as a real magnet?
options: When everyone faced a different way
When everyone faced the same way
When everyone was frozen back to back in pairs
check.why: A magnet's pull comes from many tiny magnets pointing the same way, so their pulls add up. When they face every way, the pulls cancel. When they stand back to back in pairs, like electrons in copper, they also cancel. Picking 'pairs' usually means thinking that more tiny magnets close together always means a stronger pull.

flow.do: End with one question to think about.
flow.say: WOOD, PLASTIC and BRASS did nothing. Why are those trick cards?
flow.kid: Why did WOOD and BRASS do nothing?
flow.think: When you are in a crowd, do you face the same way as everyone else? When is that good, and when is it not?

experiments.title: The Floating Needle Compass
experiments.question: Can we turn a sewing needle into a magnet, and will it point north?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a plain needle, floated on water, point any special way? And what about the same needle after you stroke it with a magnet?
experiments.fair_test: Float the needle before stroking it, and after. Use the same bowl, the same water and the same place both times. Only the stroking changes. Turn the bowl 3 times each time, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Does it pick up a pin? (yes or no)

materials.item: a steel sewing needle, about 4 to 5 cm long
a strong magnet: a bar magnet, a small round black ceramic magnet, or a small silver neodymium magnet. A bendy fridge magnet is usually too weak.
a small square of paper about 2 cm across, a small leaf, or a plastic bottle cap
a wide bowl of plastic, glass or clay, not steel, filled with water
a steel pin or small staple, to test the needle
a phone with a compass app, or a real compass, to check north

experiments.safety: Needles are sharp. A grown-up hands over the needle and puts it away afterwards. Never put magnets in your mouth.

schedule.what: Float a plain needle. Stroke it 50 times with a magnet. Float it again and see where it points. Check north.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the bowl from above, with an arrow for where the needle pointed, and write N where north is.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl with water. 2. Put it on a table at least one metre away from the gas stove, the fridge, a steel almirah, phones and other magnets. 3. Lay the plain needle on the paper square and float it in the middle.
flow.say: Let's see where a plain needle points. Iron things and phones nearby could fool it, so we keep it far away from them.
flow.kid: Fill the bowl. Put it far from the fridge, the stove and phones. Lay the needle on the paper. Float it in the middle. Where does it point?
flow.parent: Hand your child the needle, and keep a pin cushion or a piece of soap to stick it in when not in use. A steel bowl can pull the needle to its side, so use plastic, glass or clay. The plain needle may point any way, or it may slowly turn a little, because a steel needle can already be slightly magnetised. That's fine. Note what it does.
flow.context: This is the first step of the floating needle compass. Here you float a plain needle on water to see whether it points any special way.

flow.do: 1. Touch the plain needle to a pin. Does it pick the pin up? 2. Write the answer in the table.
flow.say: Is the needle a magnet yet? Let's test it on a pin.
flow.kid: Touch the needle to a pin. Does the pin stick? Write yes or no.

ask.q: Why does the plain needle not pick up the pin?
good: Its tiny magnets point every which way, so they cancel.

flow.do: 1. Lay the needle on the table. 2. Hold one end of the magnet. 3. Slide the magnet along the needle from the eye to the point. 4. Lift the magnet high in a loop and bring it back to the eye. 5. Repeat 50 times, always from eye to point, never back and forth.
flow.say: Every stroke tugs more of the tiny magnets inside the needle to point the same way. If we rub back and forth, we undo each stroke. So always one way, and lift high to come back.
flow.kid: Stroke the magnet along the needle, from the eye to the point. Lift it high. Go back to the eye. Again. Count to 50. Always the same way!
flow.parent: Hold the needle down at the eye end with one finger, and stroke away from your finger, so nobody gets poked. Counting in fives or tens helps. 5 rounds of 10 strokes is 50.

flow.do: Touch the stroked needle to the pin again.
flow.say: Now let's test it. Is it a magnet?
flow.kid: Touch the needle to the pin again. Does the pin stick now?

check.q: After 50 strokes, the needle picks up a pin. What changed inside the needle?
options: The magnet rubbed some of its magnet stuff onto the needle
The tiny magnets inside the needle now point the same way
The needle got hot from the rubbing
check.why: Nothing passed from the magnet to the needle. The stroking tugged the needle's own tiny magnets, its domains, to point the same way, so their pulls added up. Picking 'rubbed some magnet stuff on' is a very natural guess, and people believed it for centuries. But the magnet is not any weaker afterwards. Picking 'got hot' mixes this up with friction. Heat actually takes magnetism away.

flow.parent: If the pin does not stick, your magnet is probably weak. Try 50 more strokes, or a stronger magnet. A small staple or a short piece of thin wire is lighter than a pin and easier to lift.

flow.do: 1. Float the stroked needle on its paper in the middle of the bowl. 2. Wait about 30 seconds, until it stops turning. 3. Gently turn the bowl a quarter turn, and wait again. 4. Do this 3 times, writing where it points each time.
flow.say: Let's float it and wait. Then we'll turn the bowl and see if the needle turns back.
flow.kid: Float the needle again. Wait until it stops. Turn the bowl a little. Wait. Does the needle turn back the same way? Try 3 times.
flow.parent: The needle often drifts to the edge of the bowl and sticks there, because water climbs up the side. Gently push the paper back to the middle with a pencil, without touching the needle. A wider bowl helps. It should settle pointing roughly north and south each time.

flow.do: 1. Check north with a phone compass app or a real compass. Keep the phone at least half a metre from the bowl, because phones have magnets. 2. No phone? In the morning, stand facing the Sun. North is roughly to your left.
flow.say: Which end points north? Let's check with the phone, from a little way away.
flow.kid: Check where north is. Use a phone compass, but keep the phone away from the bowl. Or face the morning Sun. North is to your left. Is your needle pointing north and south?

check.q: Why does the stroked needle always turn back to point north and south?
options: It is pulled by the Pole Star
It is a magnet, and the whole Earth is a giant magnet that lines it up
The water flows north
check.why: The needle is now a magnet. The Earth is a giant magnet too, made by moving liquid iron deep inside it. The Earth's magnet turns the needle until it lines up north and south. Picking the Pole Star usually comes from knowing that the Pole Star is in the north. But stars do not pull compasses. A compass works on cloudy days and in closed rooms.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a needle stroked with a magnet becomes a magnet, and a floating magnet points north. What I saw: the plain needle did not pick up the pin. After 50 strokes it did. When I floated it and turned the bowl, it turned back to north and south three times. Why: stroking lined up the tiny magnets inside the needle, and the Earth's magnet turns it to point north.

experiments.context: In this experiment you turn a sewing needle into a magnet by stroking it. Then you float it on water and watch it find north, like the iron fish compasses sailors used long ago.

experiments.title: The Paper Clip Chain: which magnet is strongest?
experiments.question: Which of our magnets is strongest?
experiments.predict: Before you test, line up your magnets. Put the one you think is strongest first, and the weakest last. Is the biggest one the strongest?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind and size of paper clip for every magnet. Hang the chain from the same end of each magnet. Add clips one at a time, touching only the bottom clip. Test each magnet 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 2 to 4 different magnets, for example a bendy fridge magnet, a round ceramic magnet and a bar magnet
about 20 plain steel paper clips, all the same size, without plastic coating
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: If you use small neodymium magnets, keep them away from children under 5. Two swallowed magnets can pinch the gut and are an emergency. Keep magnets away from phones and bank cards.

schedule.what: Guess which magnet is strongest. Build a paper clip chain on each magnet 3 times. Fill in the table and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each magnet, as tall as its middle value.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnets in a row. 2. Ask your child to line them up from strongest to weakest, by guessing.
flow.say: Which magnet do you think is strongest? Line them up. Is the biggest one always the strongest?
flow.kid: Put your magnets in a line. Strongest first. Is the biggest one the strongest? Guess!

ask.q: Why did you put that magnet first?
good: It snaps onto the fridge hard.

flow.context: This is the first step of the paper clip chain test. You find out which magnet is strongest by counting how many clips it can hold in a chain.

flow.do: 1. Hold a magnet in the air, over the table. 2. Touch one paper clip to its bottom end, so it hangs. 3. Touch a second clip to the bottom of the first. 4. Keep adding clips, one at a time, touching only the bottom one. 5. When a clip will not stay on, stop. Count the clips that are hanging. 6. Do this 3 times for each magnet.
flow.say: Each clip becomes a little magnet, for as long as it touches the chain. That's why it can hold the next clip. How long a chain can each magnet hold?
flow.kid: Hang one clip from the magnet. Touch another clip to its bottom. And another. When one falls, stop and count. Try each magnet 3 times.
flow.parent: Hold the magnet still, and don't let the clips touch the table. A bendy fridge magnet may hold no clips at all in a chain, or just one. That is a real result. Write 0 or 1. A ceramic magnet often holds 3 to 6. A small neodymium magnet can hold 10 or more. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each magnet.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. The taller the bar, the stronger the magnet.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each magnet. Make it as tall as its middle number. A taller bar means a stronger magnet.

check.q: A big fridge magnet held 1 clip. A tiny silver magnet held 12 clips. What does this show?
options: Bigger magnets are always stronger
A small magnet can be much stronger than a big one
The tiny magnet was cheating
check.why: Strength depends on what the magnet is made of and how well its tiny magnets are lined up, not on its size. Neodymium magnets are made of iron, neodymium and boron, packed with lined-up tiny magnets. Bendy fridge magnets are mostly rubber with a little magnet powder, set in stripes. Picking 'bigger is stronger' is a very natural guess. It is true only for magnets made of the same stuff.

chart.title: Made-up example results: paper clips held in a chain
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Hang a chain of 3 clips from the strongest magnet. 2. Hold the top clip with your fingers. 3. Slowly pull the magnet away from the top clip. Watch the chain.
flow.say: What happens to the chain when the magnet leaves?
flow.kid: Hold the top clip. Pull the magnet away slowly. What happens to the other clips?

ask.q: Why did the clips fall apart when the magnet left?
good: They were only magnets while the magnet was there.
Their tiny magnets went back to pointing every which way.

flow.think: A clip was a magnet only while it touched a magnet. Are there things you can do only when someone is with you?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the small neodymium magnet is the strongest, even though it is the smallest. What I saw: it held 12 clips in a chain, and the big fridge magnet held only 1. Why: strength comes from what a magnet is made of and how its tiny magnets are lined up, not from its size.

experiments.title: Black Sand: find the magnet stone in your soil
experiments.question: Is there magnetic iron hiding in ordinary sand and soil?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you drag a magnet through sand from outside, will anything stick to it? What colour will it be?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same magnet, wrapped the same way, for every sample. Drag it the same number of times, 10, through each. Compare sand from 2 or 3 different places.
results_table: Where the sand or soil came from
How much stuck? (none, a little, a lot)

materials.item: the strongest magnet you have
a small zip bag or thin plastic bag, to wrap the magnet in
a cup of dry sand or soil from 2 or 3 places: the garden, a building site, a riverbank, a beach or a pot plant
a sheet of white paper
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: Always wrap the magnet in plastic first. Black sand stuck straight onto a strong magnet is very hard to clean off. Wash your hands after touching soil. Collect sand from a building site only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Collect dry sand or soil. Drag a wrapped magnet through it. Drop the black grains onto paper and look closely.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what the grains looked like under the magnifying glass.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, collect a cup of dry sand or soil from 2 or 3 different places. 2. If it is wet, spread it on newspaper in the sun for an hour first.
flow.say: We're going hunting for the magnet stone that people found long ago. It might be hiding in ordinary sand.
flow.kid: Collect a cup of dry sand from 2 or 3 places. Wet? Dry it in the sun first. You are hunting for magnet stone!
flow.context: This is the first step of the black sand experiment. You collect sand or soil to search for tiny grains of magnetite, the mineral that lodestones are made of.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnet inside the zip bag. 2. Pour the first sample onto a plate. 3. Drag the wrapped magnet slowly through it 10 times. 4. Lift it up and look.
flow.say: Wrap the magnet first, so we can get the grains off later. Now drag it through slowly.
flow.kid: Put the magnet in the bag. Drag it through the sand 10 times, slowly. Lift it up. What is stuck to it?
flow.parent: Most Indian sand and soil has some magnetite, which shows as a fuzzy black beard on the bag. River sand used for building, and dark beach sand, especially in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, usually have a lot. Red soil from the garden may give only a few grains. If nothing sticks, try a stronger magnet, drier sand, or sand from a building site or a drain edge.

flow.do: 1. Hold the bag over the white paper. 2. Pull the magnet out of the bag. 3. The black grains drop onto the paper.
flow.say: Watch what happens when the magnet leaves the bag.
flow.kid: Hold the bag over white paper. Pull the magnet out of the bag. The grains fall off! Look at them with a magnifying glass.

ask.q: What do the grains look like?

flow.do: Test the other samples the same way. Write down how much stuck each time.
flow.say: Which place had the most black sand?
flow.kid: Test your other sand the same way. 10 drags each. Which had the most black grains?

check.q: The black grains stuck to the magnet. What are they?
options: Bits of the magnet that broke off
Magnetite, a mineral with iron in it
Ordinary sand that got dirty
check.why: The black grains are magnetite, a mineral made of iron and oxygen. A magnet pulls it because of the iron. Lodestones, the natural magnets people found long ago, are made of magnetite too. Picking 'bits of the magnet' is a fair guess, but the magnet was wrapped in plastic. Ordinary light sand grains are mostly quartz, which is not magnetic, so they fall off.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: ordinary sand has tiny grains of magnetic iron in it. What I saw: black grains stuck to the wrapped magnet, but the light-coloured sand fell off. The building-site sand gave the most. Why: the black grains are magnetite, which has iron in it, and magnets pull iron.

experiments.context: In this experiment you drag a wrapped magnet through sand and soil. You find tiny black grains of magnetite, the same mineral that the first magnet stones were made of.

activities.title: Guess, Then Test: what does a magnet pull?

materials.item: a magnet
8 small things: a steel pin, a brass key or diya, a copper coin or wire, aluminium foil, a steel spoon, a coin, a pencil, a paper clip

activities.safety: Keep pins in a small bowl so they don't get lost on the floor.

schedule.what: Sort 8 things into 'will stick' and 'won't stick' by guessing. Then test each one.

activities.record: Put a tick next to each guess that was right.

flow.do: 1. Lay the 8 things on the table. 2. Ask your child to put them in two piles: 'I think it will stick' and 'I think it won't'.
flow.say: Before we test anything, let's guess. Which of these will a magnet pull?
flow.kid: Look at the 8 things. Make two piles. Will stick. Won't stick. Just guess!

ask.q: Why did you put the metal things in the 'will stick' pile?

flow.context: This is the first step of a quick guessing game. You guess which things a magnet will pull, and then test them.

flow.do: Test each thing with the magnet, one at a time.
flow.say: Now test each one. Were you right?
flow.kid: Now test each one with the magnet. Were you right?

check.q: The brass key and the copper coin did not stick, but the steel pin did. What does this show?
options: The magnet is broken
Only some metals are magnetic
Shiny things don't stick
check.why: Magnets pull only metals with iron, nickel or cobalt in them. Steel is mostly iron, so the pin sticks. Brass and copper have no iron, so they don't. Picking 'shiny things don't stick' is a good try at a pattern, but a shiny steel spoon may stick and a dull iron nail does.

flow.parent: Your child will probably expect every metal to stick. The surprise is the point. Steel spoons and tumblers may or may not stick, depending on the steel. Indian coins differ too. Don't give away the answer before the test.

flow.do: Leave your child with a question.
flow.say: So what is it about the pin that the key doesn't have? That's what we'll find out.
flow.kid: The pin stuck. The key didn't. Both are metal. Why? Keep that question in your head!
flow.think: What could be inside a pin that isn't inside a key?

activities.context: This is a quick guess-and-test activity to start the unit. You guess which things a magnet pulls, and get a surprise about metals.

activities.title: Draw the Invisible: the shape of a magnet's pull

materials.item: the black sand you collected in the black sand experiment, or iron filings
a bar magnet, or the strongest magnet you have
a sheet of stiff white paper or thin card, and a pencil
two books of the same thickness

activities.safety: Never put the black sand or filings straight onto the magnet. Keep them on the paper. Wash your hands afterwards and keep filings away from eyes.

schedule.what: Lay paper over a magnet, sprinkle black grains, tap, and draw the pattern.

activities.record: Draw the pattern you see. Mark the two places where the grains bunch up most.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnet on the table between two books. 2. Lay the paper over the books, so it sits just above the magnet without touching it. 3. Sprinkle a thin layer of black grains across the middle of the paper.
flow.say: A magnet's pull is invisible. But the black grains are tiny magnets when they're near it. They'll line up and show us its shape.
flow.kid: Put the magnet between two books. Lay paper on top. Sprinkle black grains on the paper, thinly. Don't let them touch the magnet!
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Invisible. You use black sand or iron filings on paper to see the shape of a magnet's invisible pull.

flow.do: 1. Tap the paper gently with a finger, again and again. 2. Watch the grains move into lines.
flow.say: Tap gently. What shape are the grains making?
flow.kid: Tap the paper gently. Keep tapping. Watch the grains. What shape do they make?
flow.parent: Black sand gives a rougher pattern than filings, but you can still see the grains bunch at the two ends and make curved lines. Use only a thin layer. If the grains clump into a ball, there are too many. Tip some off and try again.

ask.q: Where do the grains bunch up most?
good: At the two ends of the magnet.

flow.do: Help your child draw the pattern with a pencil, then compare it to a picture of the Earth's magnetic lines.
flow.say: Scientists call this shape the magnetic field. The Earth's magnet makes this same shape, but as big as the planet.
flow.kid: Draw the lines you see. Now look at a picture of the Earth's magnetic lines. Do they look alike?

check.q: In the pattern, the grains crowd most at the two ends of the magnet. Why?
options: The pull is strongest at the ends, the poles
The grains roll there because the paper slopes
The middle of the magnet is broken
check.why: A magnet's pull is strongest at its two ends, called poles. The grains crowd there and the curved lines start and end there. Picking 'the paper slopes' is a fair check to make. Test it by turning the paper around. The pattern stays with the magnet.

flow.do: Tip the grains back into their jar using the paper as a funnel.
flow.say: Let's save the grains for next time.
flow.kid: Fold the paper into a funnel. Tip the grains back into the jar.
flow.think: The pull was there before we sprinkled the grains. Is something real if we can't see it?

activities.context: In this activity you make a magnet's invisible pull visible, using black sand or iron filings on paper above a magnet.

activities.title: The Magnet Timeline on a String

materials.item: a piece of string about 3 metres long
12 small cards or pieces of paper, and crayons
clothes pegs or tape

activities.safety: Tie the string low, below a child's shoulder, so nobody walks into it.

schedule.what: Make 12 history cards and hang them on a string in order.

activities.record: Take a photo of the finished timeline, or draw it.

flow.do: Help your child write and draw one card for each event: about 600 BCE Thales and the lodestone in Greece. About 240 BCE the Chinese 'loving stone'. The Sushruta Samhita's magnet for arrowheads in India. 1044 the Chinese south-pointing iron fish. 1088 Shen Kuo's needle. About 1232 al-Awfi in Delhi describes the floating fish. 1269 Peregrinus and the two poles. 1600 Gilbert says the Earth is a magnet. 1820 Oersted's twitching compass. 1897 Marie Curie studies magnets in steel. 1936 Inge Lehmann finds the solid core. 1975 magnetic bacteria described.
flow.say: Let's make a timeline of how people learned about magnets. One card for each discovery, with a little drawing.
flow.kid: Make 12 cards. Each one is a magnet discovery. Write the year and draw a little picture.
flow.parent: The Sushruta Samhita is hard to date exactly. It was written down over many centuries, and the version we have is more than 1,500 years old. Put it between 240 BCE and 1044 with a question mark. BCE years count backwards: 600 BCE is earlier than 240 BCE.
flow.context: This is the first step of the magnet timeline. You make cards for discoveries about magnets, from ancient Greece, China and India to today.

flow.do: 1. Tie the string across a room, low down. 2. Peg the cards on in order, oldest on the left.
flow.say: Which is oldest? Which is newest? Let's put them in order.
flow.kid: Hang the cards on the string. Oldest on the left. Newest on the right.

options: William Gilbert saying the Earth is a magnet, in 1600
Shen Kuo describing a magnet needle, in 1088
Marie Curie studying magnets in steel, in 1897
check.why: 1088 is the smallest of the three years, so Shen Kuo came first. Gilbert came 512 years later, in 1600, and Marie Curie in 1897. Picking Gilbert is common, because many Western books start the story of magnets with him. The Chinese, Indian and Islamic stories come earlier.

flow.do: Stand back and look at the whole timeline together.
flow.say: Look at the places on our cards. Greece, China, India, Delhi, France, England, Denmark. What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Look at all the places on your cards. Did one country find out everything?
flow.think: Two women are on our timeline. Can you find out about other women who studied magnets?

activities.context: In this activity you hang a timeline of magnet discoveries across a room. It shows how people in many countries added to what we know.
