activities.title: Gilbert's Little Earth: a needle on a thread

materials.item: the magnetised needle from the floating compass experiment, or a newly stroked one
a piece of sewing thread about 30 cm long
a bar magnet or round magnet
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up ties the thread to the needle.

schedule.what: Hang a magnetised needle on a thread. Walk it around a magnet and draw where it points.

activities.record: Draw the magnet in the middle of the paper, and an arrow at each place for where the needle pointed.

flow.do: 1. Tie the thread around the middle of the needle. 2. Slide the knot until the needle hangs level. 3. Hold the thread up, far from any iron. Watch the needle settle.
flow.say: This hanging needle is a compass. Watch it settle north and south.
flow.kid: Hang the needle on its thread. Keep it far from iron. Wait. Which way does it settle?
flow.context: This is the first step of Gilbert's Little Earth. In 1600, William Gilbert moved a tiny compass around a magnet ball. Here you do the same with a needle on a thread.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnet in the middle of the paper. 2. Hold the hanging needle about a hand's width from the magnet, at 8 places around it, like the numbers on a clock. 3. At each place, wait for it to settle and draw an arrow the way it points.
flow.say: Move the needle around the magnet slowly. Each time, draw which way it points.
flow.kid: Hold the needle near the magnet. Move it around, like the hands of a clock. At each place, draw an arrow for where it points.
flow.parent: Closer than a hand's width, the needle may just jump onto the magnet. Further away, it starts to point north again. Your arrows should curve around the magnet, from one end to the other, like the black sand lines.

flow.do: Compare the drawing to a picture of the Earth with a compass on it.
flow.say: Gilbert saw this and thought: a compass on the Earth behaves just like this. So the Earth must be a magnet.
flow.kid: Your needle pointed along curved lines around the magnet. A compass on the Earth does the same. What did Gilbert decide?

check.q: William Gilbert's tiny compass behaved the same around his magnet ball as compasses do on the real Earth. What did he decide?
options: The Earth is a giant magnet
Compasses are attracted to the Pole Star
Magnets only work on small balls
check.why: If a compass acts the same around a magnet ball as it does on the Earth, the simplest explanation is that the Earth is a magnet too. Before Gilbert, many people thought compasses were pulled by the Pole Star or by a magnet mountain. Picking the Pole Star means following that old idea.

activities.context: In this activity you copy William Gilbert's famous 1600 experiment. You move a hanging needle compass around a magnet and draw how it points.

activities.title: Find Your Beach: be a sea turtle

materials.item: a blindfold or a soft cloth
4 cards marked WEAK, MEDIUM, STRONG, VERY STRONG, and a cushion for the beach

activities.safety: Play in a clear room or on grass. A grown-up walks beside the blindfolded child.

schedule.what: Act out a young turtle finding its way home by feeling the strength of the Earth's magnet.

activities.record: Draw the path the turtle took.

flow.do: 1. Put a cushion at one end of the room. This is the beach. 2. Lay the 4 cards on the floor in a line leading to it, WEAK furthest away and VERY STRONG next to the beach.
flow.say: A young sea turtle can't see a map. But the Earth's magnet is a little stronger, and slants a little differently, in every part of the ocean. Turtles can feel that.
flow.kid: The cushion is your home beach. The cards are how strong the Earth's magnet feels. You are a baby turtle. Can you find home by feel?
flow.context: This is the first step of Find Your Beach. You act out how young sea turtles may find their way using the Earth's magnet.

flow.do: 1. Blindfold your child at the far end. 2. Walk beside them. Each time they step near a card, whisper what it says. 3. Let them choose which way to go by whether it gets stronger or weaker.
flow.say: Weak. Medium. Getting stronger. Which way is home?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Listen to how strong the magnet feels. Stronger means you are getting closer. Find your beach!
flow.parent: This is a simple model. Real turtles seem to sense both the strength of the Earth's magnet and the angle it slants at, which together work like a map. Kenneth and Catherine Lohmann showed this with loggerhead turtles. Each beach has its own magnetic 'address'.

flow.do: Take off the blindfold and talk.
flow.say: Olive ridley turtles nest on beaches in Odisha, at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya. They come back after years at sea. They aren't doing it for us. They are living their own lives, finding their own beaches.
flow.kid: You found home without seeing! Real olive ridley turtles cross the sea to Odisha's beaches. How do you think it feels to know the way?

check.q: How do scientists think young sea turtles find their way across the ocean?
options: They follow the boats
They feel the strength and slant of the Earth's magnet
They remember the shapes of the waves
check.why: Experiments show that young turtles change direction when scientists change the magnet around them in a tank. Each part of the ocean has its own strength and slant of the Earth's magnet, like an address. Picking 'follow the boats' puts people at the centre. Turtles were crossing oceans for millions of years before there were boats.

activities.context: In this activity you act out a young sea turtle finding its way home across the ocean, by feeling how strong the Earth's magnet is.

activities.title: Paint an Aurora

materials.item: a sheet of black or dark blue paper
chalk, oil pastels or crayons in green, red, purple and white
a picture of the Earth's magnetic field, from the explanation cards

schedule.what: Paint auroras over mountains and add the Earth's magnetic lines in a corner.

activities.record: Write one sentence under your picture about what makes auroras.

flow.do: Look together at a photo of an aurora, and the picture of the Earth's magnetic lines.
flow.say: The Sun blows out tiny charged bits. The Earth's magnet steers them towards the poles. They crash into the air high up and make it glow.
flow.kid: Look at the aurora. The Sun's tiny bits are steered by the Earth's magnet. They hit the air and make it glow.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paint an Aurora. You learn what makes the lights near the poles, then paint them.

flow.do: 1. Draw dark mountains along the bottom. 2. Use the side of the chalk to sweep green curtains of light across the sky. 3. Add a little red at the top. 4. In one corner, draw the small Earth with its curved magnetic lines.
flow.say: Sweep the chalk sideways, like a curtain blowing. Green is oxygen glowing lower down. Red is oxygen glowing higher up.
flow.kid: Draw mountains. Sweep green chalk across the sky like a curtain. Add red on top. Draw a little Earth with its magnet lines in the corner.

flow.do: Write a sentence under the picture.
flow.say: What makes the aurora? Say it in one sentence.
flow.kid: Write one sentence. What makes an aurora?

check.q: Why are auroras seen mostly near the North and South Poles?
options: Because it is cold there
Because the Earth's magnet steers the Sun's tiny bits towards the poles
Because there is ice to reflect the light
check.why: The Earth's magnetic lines dip down into the Earth near the poles. The Sun's charged bits are steered along those lines, so most of them reach the air near the poles. Picking 'cold' or 'ice' links auroras with what the poles look like, not with what causes them. In May 2024, a big solar storm made auroras visible as far south as Ladakh.

activities.title: Heat Takes the Magnet Away

materials.item: a magnetised needle, from the floating compass experiment
kitchen tongs or pliers
a gas stove
a steel pin or a staple
a steel plate or tile to cool the needle on

activities.safety: Only a grown-up does the heating. Hold the needle with tongs or pliers, never fingers. The needle stays hot for a minute after it stops glowing. No gas stove? Watch the grown-up do it on a friend's stove, or skip to the last step.

schedule.what: A grown-up heats a magnetised needle until it glows. After it cools, test it on a pin. Then stroke it again.

activities.record: Write yes or no: picks up a pin before heating, after heating, and after stroking again.

flow.do: Test the magnetised needle on a pin first.
flow.say: First, let's check it's still a magnet.
flow.kid: Touch the needle to the pin. Is it still a magnet?
flow.context: This is the first step of Heat Takes the Magnet Away. A grown-up heats a magnetised needle to show that heat breaks up its tiny magnets' line-up.

flow.do: 1. Hold the needle by one end with tongs. 2. Put the other half in the hottest part of the gas flame, near the tip of the blue part. 3. Keep it there until it glows orange-red, about 30 seconds. 4. Lay it on the steel plate to cool for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Watch it glow. Heat makes the atoms jiggle. Will the tiny magnets stay lined up?
flow.kid: Stand back and watch the grown-up. The needle glows red! Heat makes its atoms jiggle hard. Wait 2 minutes for it to cool.
flow.parent: Iron loses its magnetism at about 770 degrees Celsius, when it glows dull red. A thin needle reaches this in a gas flame within a minute. Only the glowing part loses its magnet. So test the hot end against the pin.

flow.do: 1. When the needle is cool, touch its heated end to the pin. 2. Then stroke it 50 times with the magnet and test again.
flow.say: Is it still a magnet? And can we make it one again?
flow.kid: Touch the heated end to the pin. Does it stick? Now stroke it 50 times. Test again.

check.q: After heating until it glowed, the needle's end would not pick up the pin. Why?
options: The heat burned away the iron
The heat shook the tiny magnets out of line
The needle is now made of a different metal
check.why: Heat makes atoms jiggle. At about 770 degrees Celsius, iron's atoms jiggle so hard that the tiny magnets cannot stay lined up. The iron is still iron, which is why stroking can make it a magnet again. Picking 'burned away the iron' is a natural guess, because heat burns many things. But the needle is the same size and still made of steel.

flow.do: Talk about what happened.
flow.say: Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. Only the line-up changed, twice.
flow.kid: Heat broke the line-up. Stroking fixed it. Nothing was added. Nothing was taken away. Only the line-up changed.

challenges.title: The Steady Compass
challenges.problem: A floating needle compass works well on a table, but it sloshes about on a moving bus, a boat or in your hand. Design a compass that still points north while you walk around with it.
constraints: You may use only things from home.
Your compass must work while you walk slowly across the room holding it.
Test it with a phone compass, held at least half a metre away.
materials: a pin or pushpin and a cork or eraser
cardboard, tape and a small paper cup
general: Hang the needle on a thread inside a clear bottle, so the wind can't move it.
Balance the needle on the point of a pin stuck upright in an eraser. This is a dry compass, like the ones on ships.
Use a small closed jar filled almost to the top with water, so the water can't slosh.
creative: Glue the needle under a paper arrow and balance the arrow on a pin, so it is easier to read.
Sailors in the Arabian Sea floated iron fish in bowls. Later, ship compasses hung in rings that tilt, so they stay level when the ship rolls. Can you make a swinging holder?
Put a drop of cooking oil in the water instead of plain water, to slow the swinging.

flow.do: Before building, draw three ideas together.

flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas for a compass that won't slosh.

flow.do: 1. Build the best idea. 2. Walk across the room with it. 3. Check with a phone compass held away from it. 4. Improve it and test again.
flow.say: Build it and test it. Is it still pointing north while you walk?
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Walk with it. Check with a phone. Still pointing north? Make it better and try again.
flow.parent: The thread-in-a-bottle and pin-balance ideas usually work best. For the pin balance, push a pin upright through an eraser, and rest the needle's middle on its tip. A tiny dent of folded paper under the needle helps it balance. Keep phones and keys away, or the needle will turn to them.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together, then invent one more.

challenges.title: Iron-Proof: how far from iron must a compass be?
challenges.problem: In the story, a big iron pot fooled the ship's compass. Find out how far your compass must be from iron things at home before they stop fooling it. Then choose the best spot in your home for a compass station.
constraints: Use a measuring tape or a string marked every 10 cm.
Test at least 3 iron things, like a steel almirah, a gas cylinder, an iron karahi or a fridge.
Move the compass, not the heavy iron thing.
materials: a compass, or the needle on a thread
a measuring tape, or a string marked every 10 cm
general: Start right next to the iron thing. Move the compass back 10 cm at a time, until it points the same way as it does in the middle of the room.
Write down that distance for each thing.
creative: Draw a map of your home and colour a 'danger zone' around each iron thing. Where is the safe spot?
Test whether a closed laptop, a phone or a speaker fools the compass too. They have magnets inside.
Test the floor and walls. Many buildings have iron rods inside the concrete.

flow.do: 1. In the middle of the room, far from everything, see where the compass points. 2. Mark that direction on paper.
flow.say: First, where does the compass point when nothing is fooling it?
flow.kid: Stand in the middle of the room. Where does the compass point? Mark it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Iron-Proof. You measure how far a compass must be from iron things before they stop pulling its needle.

flow.do: 1. Hold the compass right next to an iron thing. 2. Move back 10 cm at a time. 3. Stop when it points the normal way again. 4. Write down the distance. 5. Do this for 3 things.
flow.say: Move back 10 centimetres at a time. When does the needle stop being fooled?
flow.kid: Start next to the iron thing. Step back 10 cm at a time. When does the needle point the normal way again? Write the distance.
flow.parent: Big iron things fool a compass from further away. A steel almirah or a fridge can disturb it from 50 cm to a metre away. A small iron karahi, perhaps 20 to 30 cm. Your numbers will differ.

check.q: A steel almirah fools the compass up to 80 cm away. An iron karahi fools it up to 25 cm away. Why the difference?

The karahi is not really iron
The compass likes almirahs
check.why: More iron means a stronger pull on the compass needle, so it reaches further before it gets too weak to notice. Picking 'the karahi is not iron' is a fair check. Test it with a magnet. If the magnet sticks, it is iron.

quiz.p: Which of these will a magnet pull?
quiz.why: Steel is mostly iron, so a magnet pulls it. Brass, aluminium and copper have no iron, nickel or cobalt, so a magnet ignores them. Picking any of the others usually means thinking all metals are magnetic.
Copper is a metal, but a magnet does not pull it. Iron, nickel and cobalt are the main magnetic metals.

quiz.p: To make a needle into a magnet, how should you stroke it?
opts: Always in the same direction, lifting the magnet away each time
quiz.why: Each stroke in the same direction tugs more of the needle's tiny magnets into line. Stroking back and forth undoes each stroke. Picking 'just once, very hard' usually means thinking force matters more than repeating the line-up.

quiz.p: A floating magnetised needle always turns to point north and south. Why?
opts: The Earth is a giant magnet that lines it up
quiz.why: The needle is a magnet, and the Earth's magnet turns it to line up north and south. Picking the Pole Star comes from an old idea. Stars do not pull compasses, and a compass works in a closed room.

quiz.p: In the paper clip chain test, a tiny magnet held 12 clips and a big fridge magnet held 1. What can you say?
opts: The big magnet is stronger, because it is bigger
The test was not fair, because the magnets were different sizes
quiz.why: More clips in the chain means a stronger magnet. Size does not decide strength. What the magnet is made of does. Picking 'not fair' is a thoughtful idea, but here the size is part of what we are comparing, not something we must keep the same.

quiz.p: In a fair test of which magnet is strongest, what should stay the same?
opts: The kind and size of paper clips
The number of clips each magnet holds
Nothing needs to stay the same
quiz.why: Everything except the magnet should stay the same, including the clips. If one magnet got smaller clips, it could hold more, and the test would not be fair. The number of clips is what we measure, so it changes.

quiz.p: Every electron is a tiny magnet. Why aren't you magnetic?
opts: Your electrons are in pairs pointing opposite ways, so they cancel
You are magnetic, but only on Sundays
quiz.why: In most atoms, electrons live in pairs, and the two in each pair point their tiny magnets opposite ways. So they cancel out. Picking 'too small' sounds sensible, but iron's electrons are just as small. The difference is whether they cancel.

opts: The two ends of a magnet
Teams of atoms inside iron whose tiny magnets point the same way
quiz.why: Domains are tiny patches inside iron, where millions of atoms point their tiny magnets the same way. In a plain nail they point different ways. In a magnet they mostly line up. Picking 'the two ends' mixes domains up with poles.

quiz.p: A magnetised needle is heated until it glows red. When it cools, it no longer picks up a pin. Why?
opts: The heat burned the iron away
The heat shook its tiny magnets out of line
Hot things are never magnetic, even after they cool
quiz.why: Heat is atoms jiggling. At about 770 degrees Celsius, iron's tiny magnets jiggle out of line, and they stay jumbled after it cools. Stroking it again can line them up again. Picking 'burned away' is natural, but the needle is still there, still steel.

opts: A natural magnet made of the mineral magnetite
A heavy iron weight on a ship
A magnet made in a factory
quiz.why: A lodestone is a piece of magnetite, a black mineral with iron in it, that is a magnet straight from the ground. People in Greece, China and India found them long ago.

quiz.p: In the old Indian surgery book, the Sushruta Samhita, what is a magnet used for?
opts: Pulling a smooth iron arrowhead out of a wound
quiz.why: The Sushruta Samhita describes using a magnet, called ayaskanta, to draw out iron arrowheads without barbs. A magnet pulls iron, but not skin. Picking 'finding north' mixes this up with the compass, which came into use later.

quiz.p: What makes the Earth a magnet?
opts: A giant bar magnet buried at the North Pole
Liquid iron moving in the Earth's outer core
The Moon pulling on the Earth
quiz.why: Liquid iron swirls slowly in the outer core, about 3,000 kilometres down. Moving metal carries electric currents, and currents make a magnet. Picking 'a giant bar magnet' is a common picture, but the core is far too hot for a solid magnet. Above 770 degrees, iron cannot stay a magnet.

quiz.p: The Earth's magnet has flipped many times, so that a compass would have pointed south.
quiz.why: True. Old lava rocks are magnetised in both directions. The last flip was about 780,000 years ago. Motonori Matuyama showed this from rocks in Japan and Korea in 1929.

quiz.p: Which of these living things has been shown to use the Earth's magnet to find its way?
quiz.why: Experiments by Kenneth and Catherine Lohmann show young loggerhead turtles change direction when the magnet around them is changed. Robins and some bacteria use it too. Picking 'only compasses can' puts our tools at the centre. Many animals had a magnetic sense long before people made compasses.

quiz.p: Do scientists know exactly how birds feel the Earth's magnet?
opts: No. The leading idea is a substance in their eyes, but it is still being tested
Birds don't feel it at all
Yes, they have a tiny compass needle in their beaks
quiz.why: The leading idea is cryptochrome, a substance in birds' eyes affected by the Earth's magnet. It is not yet fully proven. The beak idea was tested in 2012, and the iron cells there turned out to be blood cleaner cells, not magnet sensors.

items.p: Which of these will a magnet pull?
items.why: Iron is magnetic, so a magnet pulls a nail. Wood, plastic and glass are not magnetic. Picking the bangle sometimes comes from thinking shiny things are metal.
items.art: A magnet and four objects: pencil, nail, spoon, bangle.

items.p: Sort these. Will a magnet pull them?
items: a steel safety pin
Magnetic
a brass key
Not magnetic
an iron nail
Magnetic
aluminium foil
Not magnetic
a copper wire
Not magnetic
a steel paper clip
Magnetic
a rubber eraser
Not magnetic
a nickel wire
Magnetic
items.why: Things with iron, nickel or cobalt are magnetic. Brass, aluminium, copper and rubber are not.

items.p: All metals are magnetic.
items.why: False. Only metals with iron, nickel or cobalt in them are pulled. Copper, brass, aluminium, gold and silver are not.

items.p: A magnet's pull can go through paper.
items.why: True. A magnet can pull a pin through paper, cloth, wood and even your hand.

items.p: A natural magnet stone, made of magnetite, is called a ____.
items.why: Lodestones are natural magnets. People in Greece, China and India found them long ago.

items.p: A small magnet that can turn freely and points north is called a ____.
items.why: A compass is a magnet that turns until it lines up with the Earth's magnet.

items.p: You stroke a needle with a magnet 50 times, always the same way. What happens?
items.why: Stroking lines up the tiny magnets inside the needle, so it becomes a magnet. Picking 'nothing' can happen if the magnet used was a weak fridge magnet. Try a stronger one.

items.p: Why should you float the needle compass in a plastic or glass bowl, not a steel one?
opts: Some steel bowls are magnetic and would pull the needle to the side
items.why: The needle is a magnet, and a magnet pulls iron and many kinds of steel. A magnetic steel bowl would pull the needle to its edge and fool it.

items.p: Put the steps for making a needle compass in order.
items: Float it on paper in a bowl of water
Stroke the needle with a magnet 50 times, always one way
Check that the needle picks up a pin
Wait for it to stop turning, and check north
a: Stroke the needle with a magnet 50 times, always one way
Check that the needle picks up a pin
Float it on paper in a bowl of water
Wait for it to stop turning, and check north
items.why: First make the magnet, then check it worked, then float it, then read it.

items.p: In the paper clip chain test, why does each clip hold the next one?
opts: Each clip becomes a temporary magnet while it touches the chain
items.why: Near a magnet, a clip's tiny magnets line up, so it becomes a magnet too and can hold the next clip. Take the magnet away and the chain falls apart.

items.p: Where is a magnet's pull strongest?
opts: At its two ends, the poles
Only on the side with writing
items.why: A magnet's pull is strongest at its two ends, called poles. That is where the black grains crowd and where most paper clips cling.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: an end of a magnet, where the pull is strongest
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: In the story 'The Iron Fish', the compass pointed the wrong way in the storm. Why?
opts: A big iron cooking pot was tied right next to it
The rain washed its magnet away
items.why: The iron fish was a magnet, and a magnet is pulled towards iron. The big iron pot pulled its nose. When the pot was moved away, the fish pointed south again. Hidden stars made the compass needed, but did not fool it.

items.p: The black grains that stick to a magnet dragged through sand are a mineral called ____.
items.why: Magnetite is made of iron and oxygen. Lodestones are made of it too.

items.p: Why does a compass point north? Use the words 'magnet' and 'Earth' in your answer.
items.a: A compass needle is a magnet. The Earth is a giant magnet too. The Earth's magnet turns the needle until it lines up north and south.
items.why: A full answer says that both the needle and the Earth are magnets.

items.p: Draw a bar magnet with paper clips hanging from it. Show where most of the clips cling.
items.a: Most clips cling at the two ends, with few or none in the middle.
items.why: A magnet's pull is strongest at its two poles, the ends.
items.art: A blank outline of a bar magnet.

items.p: Every electron is a tiny magnet. Why is copper not magnetic?
opts: In copper, the electrons' tiny magnets cancel each other out
items.why: Copper's electrons are in pairs, or shared, so their tiny magnets cancel. Iron has electrons with no partner, so its tiny magnets don't cancel. Picking 'no electrons' misses that every atom has electrons.

items.p: A plain iron nail has millions of tiny atom-magnets. Why is it not a magnet?
opts: Its domains point in different directions and cancel out
Nails are made of wood inside
items.why: The nail's teams of tiny magnets, its domains, point every which way, so their pulls cancel. Bring a magnet near and they line up.

items.p: When you stroke a needle and it becomes a magnet, the magnet you stroked it with gets weaker.
items.why: False. Nothing passes from the magnet to the needle. The needle's own tiny magnets are lined up. You can magnetise hundreds of needles with one magnet.

items.p: Which would most likely take away a magnet's magnetism?
opts: Heating it until it glows red
items.why: Heat makes atoms jiggle. At about 770 degrees Celsius, iron's tiny magnets cannot stay lined up. Cold water and paint do not shake them.

items.p: The temperature at which a magnet stops being a magnet is called the ____ point.
items.why: It is named after Pierre Curie, who measured it in 1895. Marie Curie's first research was on magnets in steel too.

items.p: Which of these has a magnetic sense, shown by experiments?
items.why: Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko showed in 1972 that robins pick their migration direction using the Earth's magnet.

items.p: Match each person to what they found.
pairs: a compass does not point exactly north
items.why: People from many countries pieced together the story of the Earth's magnet.

items.p: Put these in time order, oldest first.
items: Gilbert says the Earth is a magnet
Shen Kuo describes a magnet needle
The Chinese book calls the magnet a 'loving stone'
Marie Curie studies magnets in steel
a: The Chinese book calls the magnet a 'loving stone'
Shen Kuo describes a magnet needle
Gilbert says the Earth is a magnet
Marie Curie studies magnets in steel
items.why: About 240 BCE, then 1088, then 1600, then 1897.

items.p: A paper clip chain test gave these middle values: fridge magnet 1, ceramic magnet 4, bar magnet 6. Which magnet is in the middle for strength?
items.why: In order, 1, 4, 6. The ceramic magnet, at 4, is in the middle.

chart.title: Paper clips held in a chain (made-up example)

items.p: Why do auroras happen mostly near the poles?
opts: The Earth's magnet steers the Sun's tiny charged bits there
items.why: The Earth's magnetic lines dip into the Earth near the poles, guiding the Sun's charged bits into the air there. They make the air glow.

items.p: A compass points exactly at the North Pole.
items.why: False. It points at the magnetic north pole, which is a different place and moves every year. Shen Kuo noticed the difference in 1088.

items.p: In the story 'The Iron Fish', Amina rubbed the fish with the stone 'from tail to nose, never back and forth'. Explain why, using the words 'tiny magnets'.
items.a: Each stroke one way pulls more of the tiny magnets inside the iron to point the same way. Rubbing back and forth would undo each stroke, so they would stay jumbled.
items.why: A good answer says that the strokes line the tiny magnets up, and back-and-forth undoes it.

items.p: Black sand from a building site gave lots of magnetite. Pot plant soil gave almost none. Give one possible reason.
items.a: River sand used for building often comes from rocks rich in magnetite. Pot plant soil is mostly old leaves and compost, with less rock in it.
items.why: Any reason about where the sand or soil came from, and what rocks it was made from, is good.

items.p: Some people sell magnet bracelets that they say cure pain. What have careful tests found?
opts: People feel about as much better with fake magnets as with real ones
items.why: When people don't know whether their bracelet is real or fake, both groups feel about the same. So the magnet itself is not doing it. A 2007 review of many tests found no good evidence.

items.p: Draw two squares of iron from very close up. In one, draw the tiny magnets as arrows for a plain nail. In the other, for a magnet.
items.a: Plain nail: patches of arrows pointing in different directions. Magnet: nearly all the arrows pointing the same way.
items.why: This shows domains: jumbled in a nail, lined up in a magnet.
items.art: Two empty squares side by side.

items.p: The Earth's core is far hotter than 770 degrees Celsius, the temperature where iron stops being a magnet. So how can the Earth be a magnet?
items.a: The Earth is not a magnet because of lined-up domains. It is a magnet because liquid iron moves in the core. Moving metal carries electric currents, and electric currents make magnets.
items.why: This joins two ideas from the unit: heat stops lined-up magnets, but moving electricity makes magnets.

items.p: Some old books say Indian sailors invented a fish compass called a 'matsya yantra'. What evidence would you need to decide whether that is true?
items.a: I would need an old Indian text or object that describes or shows the compass, with a date. Then I could compare that date with the Chinese texts from 1044 and 1088.
items.why: Good answers ask for a dated source, and compare it with other evidence.

items.p: A scientist sees that a type of bacteria always swims towards the north in a dish. She turns a magnet around the dish, and the bacteria turn too. What is the best conclusion?
opts: Bacteria can see the Pole Star
items.why: Changing only the magnet changed what the bacteria did. That is good evidence they sense magnets. These are magnetic bacteria, with tiny magnetite chains inside them.

items.p: Cows in satellite pictures seemed to face north and south. A later study found no pattern. If you were a scientist, what would you do next?
items.a: I would watch cows myself, in many places, and record which way they face. I would also record the wind and the Sun, because those could change which way they face.
items.why: Good answers repeat the study and think about other causes.

items.p: Salvatore Bellini saw magnetic bacteria in 1963, but his notes were not published. Richard Blakemore described them in 1975. Who should get credit?
opts: Only Bellini, because he was first
Both, and we should say what each did
items.why: Science usually credits whoever publishes first. But being honest means saying who saw it first, too. Bellini's notes were published in English in 2009.

items.p: Andre Geim made a live frog float in a giant magnet. The frog has no iron in it. Explain how this can be.
items.a: Everything answers a magnet a little. Water, which frogs are mostly made of, is pushed away very slightly. In a giant magnet, the push is strong enough to hold the frog up.
items.why: This shows that 'non-magnetic' really means 'very, very slightly magnetic'.

items.p: Why do scientists think Mars lost much of its air?
opts: Without a strong magnet around the planet, the solar wind stripped it away
items.why: Mars has almost no magnet around the whole planet today. Many scientists think the solar wind slowly stripped its air away. Some was frozen into ice caps, but not most of it.

items.p: A robin's magnetic sense may depend on the spins of pairs of electrons in its eye. Why is that surprising?
items.a: Electron spin is part of quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things. People thought quantum effects were too delicate to matter in a warm, living body.
items.why: Good answers mention that quantum physics is usually about tiny, cold, still things, not living birds.

items.p: Why did the Colaba magnetic observatory move from Bombay to Alibag in 1904?
opts: Electric trams were coming, and their currents would disturb the measurements
items.why: Electric currents make magnets. Bombay's new electric trams would have disturbed the delicate measurements of the Earth's magnet.

items.p: Marie Curie's first research was on magnets in steel. Find out one thing she discovered later. Why do you think her magnet work is less well known than Pierre Curie's?
items.a: She later discovered radium and polonium. Her magnet work may be less known because books often credited men's work first, and because her later work was so famous.
items.why: Any honest answer that names a later discovery and thinks about why credit is uneven is good.

items.p: Nobody has ever found a magnet with only one pole.
items.why: True. Cut a magnet in half and you get two magnets, each with two poles. Physicists have searched for single-pole magnets, called monopoles, for nearly a hundred years, and have never found one.

items.p: Design an experiment to test whether ants can sense a magnet. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would watch.
items.a: I would put ants in a round dish and watch which way they walk. Then I would put a strong magnet on one side, and later on the other side. I would keep the light, food and dish the same. I would count how many ants walk towards the magnet each time.
items.why: A good design changes only the magnet, keeps everything else the same, and counts what happens.

items.p: The Earth's magnetic north pole moves about 40 kilometres a year. If a map's compass note is 10 years old, how far might the pole have moved?
items.why: 40 kilometres each year, for 10 years, is 40 times 10, which is 400 kilometres. That is why compass maps are updated.

items.p: Many old names for magnets mean 'loving' or 'kissing'. Scientists say it is just electrons lining up. Can both be true in their own way? Explain what you think.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: the science explains how the pull works. The old names describe how it looks and feels to us. Both say that the magnet and the iron seem drawn together.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer keeps the science and the feeling clear and separate.

items.p: Draw the Earth cut in half. Label the crust, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core. Draw curved magnetic lines around the outside.
items.a: A thin crust, a thick rocky middle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, with curved lines looping from one pole round to the other.
items.why: This shows where the Earth's magnet is made, and its shape.

open_questions.q: What is an electron's spin, really?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure it very exactly and use it every day, but cannot say what it is underneath. Some think it needs no further explanation.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do birds feel the Earth's magnet?
open_questions.why_open: The leading idea is cryptochrome in their eyes, which works through electron spins. It has been shown in the lab but not yet fully proven in living birds.

open_questions.q: Can people sense the Earth's magnet, even without knowing it?
open_questions.why_open: One 2019 study found brainwave changes in some people. It has not yet been repeated by other teams.

open_questions.q: When will the Earth's magnet flip next?
open_questions.why_open: Flips don't come on a schedule. The magnet has weakened a little over the last 200 years, but that may or may not mean a flip is coming. Nobody can predict it yet.

open_questions.q: Why does the magnetic north pole move so fast, and why did it speed up and then slow down?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how the liquid iron moves deep in the core, which nobody can see directly. Scientists use computer models and argue about them.

open_questions.q: Do magnetic monopoles, magnets with only one pole, exist anywhere?
open_questions.why_open: Some theories say they should have been made just after the universe began. Physicists have searched for nearly a hundred years and found none.

open_questions.q: How exactly did lodestones become magnets?
open_questions.why_open: Lightning explains some, but maybe not all. Scientists are still studying which kinds of magnetite hold their magnet best.

open_questions.q: Why does a hot liquid core keep making a magnet for billions of years?
open_questions.why_open: The geodynamo is so complicated that computers can only copy it roughly. How the Earth's magnet first started, and how it has lasted, are still argued about.

maths.problem: In the paper clip chain test, the neodymium magnet held 12 clips. The ceramic magnet held 4 clips. How many times as many clips did the neodymium magnet hold?
maths.explain: The neodymium magnet held 12 clips and the ceramic magnet held 4. 12 divided by 4 is 3. So it held 3 times as many. Check: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
maths.context: This is about the paper clip chain test. You hang paper clips in a chain from a magnet, one at a time, and count how many it can hold before one falls.

chart.title: Paper clips held in a chain

maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'this magnet is stronger'. Dividing one number by the other tells us how many times stronger.

maths.problem: To make a needle into a magnet, you stroke it in 5 rounds of 10 strokes. How many strokes is that altogether?
maths.explain: Each round is 10 strokes. There are 5 rounds. 5 groups of 10 is 50. You can count in tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
maths.context: This is about the floating needle compass. You stroke a needle with a magnet, always the same way, to turn it into a magnet.
maths.why_maths: Counting 50 strokes one by one is easy to lose. Counting in equal groups of 10 keeps your place.

maths.problem: The Chinese book Wujing Zongyao described an iron fish compass in 1044. William Gilbert said the Earth is a magnet in 1600. How many years apart are they?
maths.explain: Take the earlier year from the later year. 1600 take away 1044. 1600 take away 1000 is 600. 600 take away 44 is 556. So they are 556 years apart.
maths.context: This is about the magnet timeline on a string. You make cards for discoveries about magnets and hang them in order.
maths.why_maths: A timeline shows which came first. Subtracting the years tells us how long people used compasses before anyone knew why they worked.

maths.problem: Look at the map of your home. You stand at the front door facing north. You turn to face east, then turn again to face south. How many quarter turns did you make, and which way did you turn?
maths.answer: 2 quarter turns, both to the right. That is a half turn.
maths.explain: North to east is one quarter turn to the right. East to south is another quarter turn to the right. 1 + 1 = 2 quarter turns. Two quarter turns make a half turn, so now you face the opposite way from north.
maths.context: This is about My Compass Diary, where you use a compass to mark north, east, south and west on a map of your home.
maths.why_maths: A compass only helps if you can turn its north into the other directions. Quarter turns are the maths of finding your way.

maths.problem: Look at the scale. It shows how far a compass was from a steel almirah when it stopped being fooled. Each big mark is 10 cm. Each small mark is 5 cm. What is the reading?
maths.explain: The pointer is past the 70 mark but before 80. It sits on the small mark halfway between them. Each small mark is 5 cm. 70 + 5 = 75. So the compass had to be 75 cm away.
maths.context: This is about the Iron-Proof challenge. You move a compass away from an iron thing, 10 cm at a time, until it points the normal way again.
maths.why_maths: A measuring tape only helps if you can read the marks between the numbers. That turns 'quite far' into an exact distance.

roots.context: We have been learning about magnets, and the tiny electron magnets inside iron. Now we ask what magnets tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A magnet is not a different kind of stuff. It is ordinary iron whose tiny parts all point the same way.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into 'magnets' and 'not magnets', as if the power lived in a special stone. But every electron is already a tiny magnet. A nail and a magnet are the same iron, arranged differently.
deep_truth.evidence: Stroke a needle and it becomes a magnet. Heat it red-hot and it stops. Stroke it again and it is a magnet again. Nothing was added or taken away. Only the line-up changed.

three.who_am_i: You are full of tiny electron magnets too. In you, they point every which way and cancel out.
three.what_is_life: Turtles, robins and tiny bacteria feel the Earth's magnet and find their way by it, each living its own life.
three.what_is_this_world: The whole Earth is a magnet, made by a sea of moving iron far beneath your feet.

roots.thread: Inside a plain nail, countless tiny magnets point every way. Their pulls add up to zero, a perfect balance. Nothing seems to be there. Line them up, and one pull appears out of that zero. That one pull then reaches out to many things: a pin, a needle, a ship's course, a turtle's journey and the lights in the sky. DeepKids sees in this a small picture of the One becoming the many, where nothing new is made, only arranged.

science.text: Every electron is a tiny magnet. In most atoms they pair up and cancel. In iron, they line up in domains.
Electricity, magnetism and light are one force, electromagnetism. Maxwell joined them in 1865.
What an electron's spin is, underneath, has no agreed answer.

other_view.view: Lining up is simply how electrons in iron behave. It is a beautiful fact, but it is not a message about agreeing, or about oneness. Reading lessons into iron says more about us than about iron. That is an honest view.

practice.title: Be the needle
practice.say: Let's stand up and close our eyes. Without peeking, point to where you think north is. Now open your eyes and check with the compass. Now let's all turn to face north together. playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Changes made: bendy fridge magnets are often too weak to magnetise a needle and hold 0 or 1 clips, so the needle compass now asks for a bar, ceramic or neodymium magnet and says what to do if the pin won't lift. The floating needle uses a plastic, glass or clay bowl, because some steel bowls are magnetic, and the bowl sits a metre from the stove, fridge, almirah and phones. The needle often drifts to the bowl's edge, so the step says to nudge the paper back with a pencil. North is checked with a phone held half a metre away, or by facing the morning Sun. The black sand test wraps the magnet in a plastic bag, because magnetite stuck straight onto a strong magnet is very hard to clean, and it says which sands give most and what to try if nothing sticks. The heat activity needs a gas stove and a grown-up with tongs, and gives an alternative for homes with induction cooktops. The paper clip chain needs plain steel clips, all the same size. Parents should know: small neodymium magnets must be kept from children under 5, because two swallowed magnets can pinch the gut. Indian coins differ, and some are magnetic, which is a good surprise, not a mistake. Both games work for one child alone. Monsoon Voyage races the storm cloud, and Magnet Says uses 12 paper arrows. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.
